Q: Best practices for structuring LLM prompts to extract multi-dimensional emotional metadata from dream narratives? A:

For extracting structured psychological metadata from subjective text like dream narratives, a Schema-First + Few-Shotapproach works best. Here's what I'd recommend:

1. Define your schema explicitly upfront

Use Pydantic or a JSON schema definition in the prompt so the model knows exactly what structure to return before it reads the dream text. This drastically reduces hallucinated keys.

python

from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import List

class DreamAnalysis(BaseModel):
    emotional_intensity: float  # 0.0 to 1.0
    key_archetypes: List[str]
    sentiment_trend: str  # "positive-to-negative", "stable", etc.
    summary: str

2. Chain your prompts — don't do it all in one

Split into two calls:

  • Call 1: Extract raw emotional descriptors and narrative arc

  • Call 2: Map those to your schema

Single-call extraction on ambiguous text is where hallucinations creep in.

3. Few-shot examples with edge cases

Include one clear dream example and one fragmented/abstract one in your prompt. This teaches the model how to handle the non-linear metaphors you're dealing with.

4. Constrain with JSON mode

Use Gemini's response_mime_type: "application/json" or OpenAI's response_format: {"type": "json_object"} — this forces valid JSON output and reduces structural drift.

Q: Faster way to list all files in directory? A:

On unix-alikes we might use system() to call find.

fs_index_sys <- \(wd, recursive=FALSE) {
  depth <- if (recursive) "" else "-maxdepth 1"
  cmd <- sprintf(
    "find %s -printf '%%f\\t%%T@\\t%%s\\t%%p\\n'", 
    shQuote(wd)
  )
  x <- system(cmd, intern=TRUE)
  df <- read.delim(
    text=x, 
    sep='\t', 
    header=FALSE, 
    quote="", 
    col.names=c("file_name", "mtime", "size", "full_path"), 
    colClasses=c("character", "numeric", "numeric", "character")
  )
  df$date_created <- as.POSIXct(df$mtime, origin="1970-01-01")
  df$mtime <- NULL
  df$parent_folder <- dirname(df$full_path)
  df$extension <- sub("^.*\\.", "", df$file_name)
  df$extension[!grepl("\\.", df$file_name)] <- ""
  df
}

I used recursive=FALSE as default, set TRUE for all subdirectories. The columns can be expanded as desired.

Gives

Benchmark

fs_index_R <- \(wd) {
  files <- list.files(path=wd, recursive=TRUE, full.names=TRUE)
  info <- file.info(files)
  data.frame(
    file_name=basename(files), 
    date_created=info$ctime, 
    size=info$size, 
    extension=tools::file_ext(files), 
    parent_folder=dirname(files), 
    full_path=files, 
    stringsAsFactors=FALSE
  )
}

fs_index_fs <- \(wd) {
  fs::dir_info(wd, recurse=TRUE, fail=FALSE)
}

wd <- '/home/jay/Downloads'

> microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
+   fs_index_R(wd), 
+   fs_index_sys(wd, TRUE), 
+   fs_index_fs(wd), 
+   times=3L
+ )

  fs_index_fs(wd) 2222.97897 2712.30972 2882.19211 3201.64046 3211.79868 3221.95689     3   b

fs_index_sys() is about 30% faster than OP base R approach. Not sure why the advertised fs::dir_info() runs so slowly on my system.

where fs_index_sys() seems to be more/most complete:

> fs_index_R(wd) |> dim()
[1] 4756    6
> fs_index_sys(wd, TRUE) |> dim()
[1] 4784    6
> fs_index_fs(wd) |> dim()
[1] 4775   18

Q: Where are the inherited additional dependencies defined in a C++ project in Visual Studio and filled in during linking? A:

As I mentioned above, the additional libraries are included based on settings (explicit or implicit) in your project. In some cases adding a header file will create a reference to a required library that is automatically included. This is all handled automatically by Visual Studio. There are certain system files which are in the Visual Studio installation which list the ones required for different application types (Windiows, C++/CLI, Console etc.), which you can examine for yourself; on my installation of Visual Studio 18, they are at C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\18\Community\MSBuild\Microsoft\VC\v180.

Q: How to cryptographically prove a file existed at a specific time? A:

Many certificate authorities also have an adjacent "Time-Stamping Authority" (TSA) service, where instead of signing a certificate, they sign a provided hash of some arbitrary data. The signature is verifiable using the TSA's certificate chain.

Such timestamping services are commonly used for Authenticode signing (i.e. signing Windows EXE/MSI/DLL files) – the time­stamp service's counter-signature is what prevents a signed .exe from suddenly becoming invalid when the developer's certificate expires a year later. (You can right-click an .exe and go to "Digital Signatures > Details" to see the counter-signature with the CA's time­stamp in addition to the signer's self-asserted time­stamp.)

For example, DigiCert and Sectigo provide public TSA services, as do Apple1 and Microsoft – all nominally for code-signing purposes but they don't really care what hash you give them.

All these services use the RFC 3161 protocol and you can use python-rfc3161 or OpenSSL::​Time­stamp or openssl ts to generate the requests (to submit via HTTP POST) and/or verify the returned time­stamps. Of course, if your "build artifact" is an .exe/.dll/.msi file, then you already have time-stamping built into signtool.

(It seems RFC 3161 has evolved into ANSI ASC X9.95. I don't know where that's used.)

Similar services are also used for eIDAS "qualified document signing" in the XAdES/PAdES/CAdES specifications, where you have a whole set of specifications detailing what kind of auxiliary data (e.g. certificate chains, OCSP responses) must be bundled together with the document to make it fully verifiable offline two decades later.

I don't know if that's common elsewhere in the world, but in my corner of Europe a "digitally-signed contract" would come either as a PAdES-format signed PDF document, or a plain PDF inside XAdES ASiC-E archive, either way with the timestamp and all verification metadata (both for the signer and for the TSA) bundled in the document.

The ¤AdES formats are complex (and the "qualified" time­stamping services generally paid-access), but they are a wheel already invented – so if you actually want to timestamp a contract, I'd strongly recommend first looking into whether any such format has already been adopted by law in your region or jurisdiction or whatever.

Keep in mind also that just like there are different lists of "trusted CAs" for different purposes, there are also different lists of "trusted TSAs", so you need to keep your future audience in mind. For example, many of the TSAs which are in the eIDAS TSL are not built-in to the Windows CA/TSA store – and vice versa, many TSAs commonly trusted for Authenticode purposes won't be in the eIDAS TSL. (And alternative methods like Bitcoin "blockchain time­stamping" are in neither.) Ultimately, no matter the method, you will have to convince the verifier that your chosen TSA (or blockchain or whatever) is indeed trusted for time­stamping.

(Among other less-standard variants, there seems to be a long-running service providing PGP-based time­stamps. A decade ago, before the big blockchain craze, there was a company named "Guardtime" specializing in time­stamping services – once a month, instead of a CA certificate, they used to publish a Merkle Tree root hash in a newspaper as physical proof that all "leaf" hashes had existed before the paper was printed.)

1 Doesn't seem like they document it publicly though, but http://timestamp.apple.com/ts01 is what they use for "notarization" of macOS software.

Q: How to fix an error message when installing mod_wsgi? A:

First you have to determine if your Python version is 32 bits or 64 bits. It usually shows when launching python from Powershell :

C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\18\BuildTools>python
Python 3.12.0 (tags/v3.12.0:0fb18b0, Oct  2 2023, 13:03:39) [MSC v.1935 64 bit (AMD64)] on win32
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>>

One other way possible, among many, is to launch python with the verbose option : python -v . Check the output, if it launches from c:\Program Files it it 64 bits, if it launches from c:\Program Files (x86) then it is 32 bits.

Once you have determined this, you can proceed to launch the corresponding Command Prompt for VS :

Launching the 64 bit version will be a bit misleading as it will say that the environment is set for x64 but you will end up in C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\18\BuildTools . Trust the first message about the environment.

C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\18\BuildTools>
